title: Jacob Nyvall (1894−1961)
name: Jacob Nyvall
description: Jacob Nyvall was born on 23 July 1894 in Nybro, Madesjö parish and died on 1 July 1961 in Stockholm. He obtained degrees in organ performance, music teaching and as precentor from the the Royal Conservatory of Music in Stockholm, and studied composition and counterpoint with Ernst Ellberg and Andreas Hallén. From 1920 until his retirement in 1959 he was organist at Solna Church and singing teacher at elementary schools in Solna. Nyvall wrote music primarily for use in church: solo songs, choral works and organ music. He was also a music journalist.

biography: Life Jacob Nyvall was born on 23 July 23 1894 in Nybro, Madesjö parish. His first musical experiences were within the Mission Covenant Church of Sweden. After completing preparatory studies in organ under the Kalmar cathedral organist in 1911, he commenced studies at the Kungliga Musikkonservatoriet (Royal Conservatory of Music) in Stockholm, where he completed his degrees as organist in 1915 and as precentor and music teacher in 1919. He also studied counterpoint at the Conservatory under Ernst Ellberg and composition and orchestration under Andreas Hallén. From 1920 until his retirement in 1959, Nyvall worked as cathedral organist at Solna Church (obtaining permanent employment status in 1932) and as a vocal teacher at the Solna elementary schools. In 1960 he was awarded the Kungliga Patriotiska sällskapet's (Royal Patriotic Society) gold medal. Countless reports in the press bear witness to numerous church ceremonies at which Nyvall often performed the vocal solos himself. Included among the major occasions, for which he also wrote the music, are the baptisms of the Princesses Birgitta and Christina, in addition to the 80 th birthday celebration of King Gustav V. Nyvall was a also a prolific author. For several decades he reviewed newly published music in the Swedish Mission Church Vocal Society’s magazine Sångarbladet . He was also a member of the editorial staff at both Kyrkosångsförbundet and Svenskt gudstjänstliv and periodically wrote reviews for the newspaper Svenska Morgonbladet . After a brief illness, Nyvall died 1 July 1961 at Mörby Hospital. Compositions Nyvall wrote mainly vocal and organ music for use in church. His first songs were published in 1912 and altogether about 40 of his solo songs were printed. For a long time, his most frequently sung songs were ‘ Davids 23:e psalm ’ (1929), ‘Så älskade Gud världen ’ (1931) and ‘ Ett verktyg i Herrens hand ’ (1937). Besides his spiritual songs, other themes include pastoral poetry such as in ‘ Vårlåt ’ (1918) and ‘ I knoppningstider ’ (1928), village romance as in ‘ Ålänningens sång ’ (1920) and ‘ Haga ’ (1929) and patriotism in ‘ Vår Fana ’(1929) and ‘ Sång till Sverige ’ (1929). Among his over 30 published choral works there are some in motet style as well as simple hymns. For special ceremonial occasions, Nyvall wrote cantatas for chorus, soloists and instruments, ranging from the re-opening of Solna Church in 1928 to the anniversary of the youth federation (1952) − with rather antiquated lyrics. For his own personal use Nyvall composed several preludes and chorale adaptations for organ. Some appeared in print, such as the chorale partitas ‘ Jesus är min hägnad ’ (1939) and ‘ Vår blick mot helga berget går ’ (1940). Unpublished works from his student years include works for string quartet and quintet, in addition to expressive piano pieces composed during his youth. Nyvall’s production includes a large number of children’s songs and hymn tunes. His 23 barnvisor för svenska skolor och hem was published in 1925 and several songs later appeared in the Lek och allvar series , published by the Swedish Mission Covenant Society. Nyvall’s melodies were included in the Society’s Juniorsånger (1929) as well as the Supplement till Svenska Missionsförbundets sångbok (1925) and Sånger och psalmer (1951). ‘ I Herrens barmhärtiga händer ’ (1950) is still present in the more contemporary Psalmer och Sånger (1987, No. 628). Several of his children’s songs were also a part of the enduring classic Nu ska vi sjunga (1948), in which perhaps his most well-known melody is ‘ Det snöar, det snöar ’. Musical style Nyvall’s reviews as a music critic attest to a stylistic ideal that exists somewhere in between the ‘harsh’ sounds of modern contemporary music and a simpler banal style inherent to particular spiritual songs. Based on his experiences from both the Free and Swedish Churches, in an article on spiritual song in Sångarbladet (1943) Nyvall writes of how he was forced to wrestle with the ‘tension between songs’ subjective mood and the objective artistic principles of style.’ His vision as a composer was to ‘arrive at an inner synthesis, which provides the solution to the sacred vs. style problem.’ In a 1948 debate on children’s song, Nyvall still pleaded for ‘the natural’ in the form of simple melodies with harmonic accompaniment. If Late Romanticism was the starting point for his early composing, several of his songs reflect even further back, to the classical Romantic style of the 1800’s, which thrived well into the 1900’s within the Free Church. Several of his solo songs composed for use within the church have a more ‘objective’ character, with scaled-down harmonies and short, chorale-like phrases ending with cadences. His music for organ and sections of his choral music are linear with independent voices and feature abundant counterpoint characterised by imitation, canons and fugues. His organ works are not only influenced by new ideals, but also forms from the Baroque. But even here, consonant harmonies prevail: ‘harsh’ dissonances are sought in vain in Nyvall’s music. © 2016 Hans Bernskiöld Trans. Thalia Thunander
